concepts.description_formal: The average rate of change of f over an interval is expressed by either difference quotient, the h form or the two point form, both of which divide a change in f by the corresponding change in the independent variable.
concepts.description_plain: An average rate is the change in the output divided by the change in the input over an interval.
concepts.name: Average rate of change as a difference quotient

concepts.description_formal: The instantaneous rate of change of f at a is the limit of a difference quotient as the increment tends to zero or as the second input tends to a, provided the limit exists.
concepts.description_plain: The rate at a point is what the average rates approach as the interval shrinks to nothing.
concepts.name: Instantaneous rate of change as the limit of a difference quotient

concepts.description_formal: The derivative of f is the function whose value at x is the limit as h tends to zero of the quotient of f(x plus h) minus f(x) by h, provided this limit exists.
concepts.description_plain: The derivative is itself a function, whose value at each input is a limit of a difference quotient there.
concepts.name: The derivative as a function defined by a limit

concepts.description_formal: For y equal to f(x), the notations dy by dx, f prime of x, and y prime denote the derivative, and the derivative can be represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally.
concepts.description_plain: The same derivative can be written in prime form, Leibniz form, or as y prime.
concepts.name: Derivative notation and its equivalent forms
concepts.notation: dy by dx; f prime of x; y prime

concepts.description_formal: The derivative of a function at a point is the slope of the line tangent to the graph of the function at that point, which with the point of tangency determines the tangent line.
concepts.description_plain: The derivative value at a point is the slope of the line touching the curve there.
concepts.name: The derivative at a point as the slope of the tangent line

concepts.description_formal: Recognising an expression as the definition of the derivative of a function whose derivative is known determines the limit as the value of that derivative at the base point.
concepts.description_plain: A limit that has the shape of a difference quotient can be read as a derivative already known.
concepts.name: Recognising a limit as a derivative of a known function

concepts.description_formal: The derivative at a point can be estimated from information given in tables or graphs, and technology can calculate or estimate the value of a derivative at a point.
concepts.description_plain: A derivative at a point can be estimated from nearby values or from the steepness of the graph.
concepts.name: Estimation of a derivative from tabular or graphical information

concepts.description_formal: If a function is differentiable at a point then it is continuous at that point; in particular a point outside the domain of f is outside the domain of f prime.
concepts.description_plain: A function that has a derivative at a point must be continuous there.
concepts.name: Differentiability implies continuity

concepts.description_formal: A continuous function may fail to be differentiable at a point of its domain, for instance where the one sided limits of the difference quotient differ or where the tangent line is vertical and has no slope.
concepts.description_plain: A continuous function can still have no derivative, at a corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent.
concepts.name: Ways a derivative fails to exist at a point of continuity

concepts.description_formal: For f(x) equal to x to the power r, the derivative is r times x to the power r minus one, obtained by direct application of the definition of the derivative or by the rule itself.
concepts.description_plain: The derivative of a power drops the exponent by one and multiplies by the old exponent.
concepts.name: The power rule

concepts.description_formal: Sums, differences, and constant multiples of functions can be differentiated using derivative rules, and the power rule combined with these properties differentiates any polynomial.
concepts.description_plain: Constants come out, constants differentiate to zero, and sums differentiate term by term.
concepts.name: Linearity of differentiation

concepts.description_formal: Specific rules give the derivatives of sine, cosine, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
concepts.description_plain: Sine, cosine, the natural exponential, and the natural logarithm each have a rule of their own.
concepts.name: Derivatives of the basic transcendental functions

concepts.description_formal: Derivatives of products of differentiable functions can be found using the product rule, which is not the product of the derivatives.
concepts.description_plain: The derivative of a product is the first times the derivative of the second plus the second times the derivative of the first.
concepts.name: The product rule

concepts.description_formal: Derivatives of quotients of differentiable functions can be found using the quotient rule, in which the numerator is the denominator times the derivative of the numerator minus the numerator times the derivative of the denominator, over the square of the denominator.
concepts.description_plain: The derivative of a quotient has a subtraction in the numerator whose order matters and the denominator squared below.
concepts.name: The quotient rule

concepts.description_formal: Rearranging tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant using identities allows differentiation using the derivative rules already available.
concepts.description_plain: Tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant are differentiated by writing them with sine and cosine and applying the quotient rule.
concepts.name: Derivatives of the remaining trigonometric functions by rewriting
